original_value: AbstractFlipped learning (FL) has had a substantial impact on higher education worldwide, prompting active dialog among educational researchers and practitioners. It is widely accepted that the value of FL lies in enabling in‐depth, learner‐centered learning experiences by offloading content delivery onto pre‐class online learning. The in‐class component is thus generally considered more critical, even though both pre‐class and in‐class elements are indispensable components of FL and practitioners are faced with the issue of under‐prepared learners. In this study, we examine the significance of pre‐class learning as a gateway to the intended benefits of FL. We aim to investigate the extent to which FL pre‐class learning influences overall FL success and what other factors affect FL pre‐class learning to ascertain the implications of designing and implementing FL pre‐class learning. A college life science course was designed and implemented with the FL model for a semester, from which data were collected and statistically analyzed. The results indicate that the influence of pre‐class learning on final FL success is significant and strong. Regarding the modality of pre‐class learning materials, learners demonstrated higher levels of performance in the weeks with video materials than during those with reading materials. Among several learner factors, self‐direction was found to significantly influence pre‐class learning performance and perceived learning readiness. The role of FL pre‐class learning to attain the intended value of FL is discussed, and theoretical and practical design implications are suggested.

result.paraphrase: Flipped learning (FL) has significantly shaped higher education around the world, sparking active discussion among educators and researchers. It is widely recognized that FL is valuable because it supports deeper, learner-centered learning by shifting content delivery to online pre-class study. As a result, the in-class portion is often viewed as more important, although both pre-class and in-class elements are essential to FL and instructors still face the challenge of learners arriving underprepared. This study investigates how important pre-class learning is as the gateway to FL’s intended benefits. We examine how much FL pre-class learning affects overall FL success, and what additional factors influence pre-class learning, in order to clarify the implications for designing and implementing FL pre-class activities. A college-level life science course was taught using the FL model for one semester, and the resulting data were collected and analyzed statistically. The findings show that pre-class learning has a strong and significant effect on final FL success. In terms of the format of pre-class materials, learners performed better in weeks using video materials than in weeks using reading materials. Among several learner-related factors, self-direction significantly affected pre-class learning performance and perceived learning readiness. The study discusses the role of FL pre-class learning in achieving FL’s intended value and offers theoretical and practical design implications.
